title: Data-driven techniques for translational neuroscience and personalized neuro-health
summary: Neurodegenexrative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease are diagnosed most reliably only after substantial, often irreversible, neuronal loss has already occurred, creating an urgent need for quantitative tools that can detect subtle, early, and individual-specific brain changes from neuroimaging data. This review surveys a broad and rapidly evolving toolkit of data-driven techniques for translational neuroscience and personalized neuro-health, organized around four complementary methodological pillars. Throughout, we emphasize how these methodologically diverse approaches converge on a common translational goal: personalized, mechanistically grounded, and clinically actionable models of individual brain health, and we close by discussing the principal open statistical, computational, and clinical challenges that remain.

AI.tldr: A review of data-driven neuroimaging techniques for detecting early, individual-specific brain changes in neurodegenerative diseases, organized around four methodological pillars, with emphasis on personalized and clinically actionable brain health models.
AI.motivation: Neurodegenerative diseases are only reliably diagnosed after substantial and often irreversible neuronal loss has occurred. There is an urgent need for quantitative tools capable of detecting subtle, early, and individual-specific brain changes from neuroimaging data.
AI.method: The paper surveys a broad toolkit of data-driven techniques for translational neuroscience and personalized neuro-health, organized around four complementary methodological pillars that converge on a common translational goal.
AI.result: The review presents a comprehensive survey of diverse data-driven approaches and demonstrates how these methodologically varied techniques converge toward personalized, mechanistically grounded, and clinically actionable models of individual brain health.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes by discussing the principal open statistical, computational, and clinical challenges that remain in achieving personalized brain health modeling for neurodegenerative disease detection.

title: An Analytically Tractable Framework for Multi-Strain Epidemics: Resolving Algebraic Complexity to Map Oscillatory Dynamics
summary: Multi-strain epidemiological systems frequently exhibit self-sustained oscillations, yet severe algebraic complexity has long obstructed a complete analytical characterization of these dynamics. Seeking to bypass these barriers, we have identified a broad, analytically tractable class of two-strain models featuring asymmetric cross-immunity that precludes secondary infections for a single strain. This targeted structural simplification allows us to derive explicit expressions for coexistence equilibria and map their stability. We show that the relative transmission advantage of secondary infections fundamentally governs the onset of robust limit-cycle oscillations, extending previous narrow-borderline results. Crucially, numerical simulations reveal a rich macroscopic landscape where small-amplitude local oscillations coexist with large-amplitude, recurrent outbreak cycles. The structural robustness of these phenomena is confirmed by incorporating effects such as waning immunity and isolation and extending the framework beyond the analytically tractable class. These findings provide a clear mechanistic explanation for multi-strain epidemic cycles and offer a highly tractable baseline for future theoretical developments.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies an analytically tractable class of two-strain epidemiological models with asymmetric cross-immunity, derives explicit coexistence equilibria, and shows that the relative transmission advantage of secondary infections governs the onset of robust limit-cycle oscillations. Numerical simulations reveal a rich landscape where small-amplitude local oscillations coexist with large-amplitude recurrent outbreak cycles, with robustness confirmed beyond the tractable class.
AI.motivation: Multi-strain epidemiological systems frequently show self-sustained oscillations, but severe algebraic complexity has long obstructed complete analytical characterization of these dynamics.
AI.method: Identifies a broad, analytically tractable class of two-strain models with asymmetric cross-immunity that precludes secondary infections for a single strain. Derives explicit expressions for coexistence equilibria and maps their stability. Extends framework beyond the tractable class by incorporating waning immunity and isolation.
AI.result: Shows that the relative transmission advantage of secondary infections fundamentally governs the onset of robust limit-cycle oscillations, extending previous narrow-borderline results. Numerical simulations reveal coexistence of small-amplitude local oscillations with large-amplitude recurrent outbreak cycles, confirmed to be structurally robust.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a clear mechanistic explanation for multi-strain epidemic cycles and offer a highly tractable baseline for future theoretical developments in the field.

title: Body size predicts how long ant workers live - but not how they age or how they die from heat
comment: 6 figures, 10 main-text tables, and 5 supplementary tables
summary: In social insects, mortality risk comprises distinct components that may not share the same predictors: lifespan duration, senescence trajectory, and thermal vulnerability. We tested these three axes in 18 Australian ant species using paired field-laboratory survival assays (2,363 cohort-day observations; 1,148 workers). Body size predicted duration (Cox HR = 0.67, p = 0.002), while colony size (p = 0.60) and the size x temperature interaction (p = 0.72) showed no detectable moderating effect. A weak but significant size x foraging-rate interaction was detected (LRT p = 0.014), suggesting that intrinsic physiology remains the most parsimonious explanation for the main size-longevity pattern, although ecological context may contribute. Senescence trajectory was associated with circadian niche rather than size: it was steepest in matinal species (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.009; matinal vs. crepuscular p = 0.002) and was uncorrelated with body mass (Spearman p = 0.32). Thermal hazard plateaued above 20 degrees C (Delta AIC = -38; p < 0.001), with elevated thermal sensitivity in Rhytidoponera (Ectatomminae) above the plateau (5% per degree C, p = 0.015). Circadian regime and lineage identity, not body size, therefore emerge as the most climate-relevant axes, although they are strongly collinear (Cramer's V = 0.85). These results show that body size captures only one dimension of mortality risk and that size-based vulnerability indices may misrank taxa when senescence and thermal sensitivity are decoupled from body size.

AI.tldr: Using paired field-laboratory survival assays across 18 Australian ant species (1,148 workers; 2,363 cohort-day observations), this study decomposes mortality risk into three axes—lifespan duration, senescence trajectory, and thermal vulnerability. Body size predicts lifespan duration but not senescence or thermal sensitivity; circadian niche predicts senescence trajectory, and lineage identity predicts thermal sensitivity. Size-based vulnerability indices may misrank taxa when these axes are decoupled from body size.
AI.motivation: Mortality risk in social insects comprises distinct components (lifespan duration, senescence trajectory, thermal vulnerability) that may share different predictors. Understanding whether body size—commonly used in vulnerability assessments—captures all these axes is critical for accurate species risk prediction in climate change contexts.
AI.method: Paired field-laboratory survival assays were conducted on 18 Australian ant species, yielding 2,363 cohort-day observations across 1,148 workers. Body size, colony size, foraging rate, circadian niche, and temperature were analyzed via Cox proportional hazards models, Kruskal-Wallis tests, Spearman correlations, and AIC-based model comparisons to test predictors of lifespan duration, senescence trajectory, and thermal sensitivity.
AI.result: Body size predicted lifespan duration (Cox HR = 0.67, p = 0.002), with no moderating effect from colony size or size-temperature interaction, though a weak size-foraging interaction was found (LRT p = 0.014). Senescence trajectory was steepest in matinal species (p = 0.009) and uncorrelated with body mass (p = 0.32). Thermal hazard plateaued above 20 degrees C (Delta AIC = -38, p < 0.001), with elevated thermal sensitivity in Rhytidoponera (5% per degree C, p = 0.015). Circadian regime and lineage were strongly collinear (Cramer's V = 0.85).
AI.conclusion: Body size captures only one dimension of ant mortality risk. Circadian niche and lineage identity, rather than body size, are the most climate-relevant axes of vulnerability. Size-based vulnerability indices may misrank taxa when senescence and thermal sensitivity are decoupled from body size, advocating for multi-axis risk assessment frameworks.

title: Ten simple rules for non-visual, reproducible and accessible bioinformatics
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures, 5 supplementary figures, 8 supplementary tables, 1 analysis ZIP file
summary:
Bioinformatics workflows rely heavily on visual representations. Quality-control plots, cell embeddings, heatmaps, genome-browser tracks, and interactive dashboards are not merely illustrations, but instruments for making analytical decisions. For blind and low-vision researchers who use screen readers, braille displays, or audio-based interfaces, these create a barrier: the evidence used to justify an analysis is often encoded in visual form, while the underlying decision remains undocumented.
  We argue that non-visual accessibility and computational reproducibility are closely aligned, as they both require analyses to be transparent and to record why decisions were made. We present ten simple rules for non-visual bioinformatics, covering plots as decision records, cautious use of AI-generated figure descriptions, accessible computing environments, text-first literate programming, structured data and metadata, compact object summaries, accessible publication formats, collaboration practices, shared community infrastructure, and accessibility as part of FAIR research. The intended audience is computational biologists and developers.
  Using single-cell RNA-seq as a running example, we show that the accessible equivalent of a plot is a structured decision record. That is, a plot companion that goes beyond storing the underlying data by also stating the purpose of the analysis and the resulting quantitative evidence and uncertainty. We argue that treating accessibility in this way makes bioinformatics more inclusive and also more transparent and auditable.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that non-visual accessibility in bioinformatics aligns with computational reproducibility, presenting ten simple rules for making analyses accessible to blind and low-vision researchers. The key concept is that plots should be accompanied by structured decision records—capturing not just data but also analysis purpose, quantitative evidence, and uncertainty—using single-cell RNA-seq as a running example.
AI.motivation: Bioinformatics relies heavily on visual representations (plots, heatmaps, genome-browser tracks) that create barriers for blind and low-vision researchers who use screen readers, braille displays, or audio-based interfaces. Visual evidence used to justify analytical decisions remains inaccessible and undocumented, excluding a group of researchers from critical decision-making processes.
AI.method: The paper proposes ten simple rules for non-visual bioinformatics, including using plots as decision records, cautious use of AI-generated figure descriptions, accessible computing environments, text-first literate programming, structured data and metadata, compact object summaries, accessible publication formats, collaboration practices, shared community infrastructure, and incorporating accessibility into FAIR principles. The central methodological proposal is the "structured decision record"—a plot companion that stores underlying data plus the analysis purpose, quantitative evidence, and uncertainty.
AI.result: Using single-cell RNA-seq as a running example, the paper demonstrates that the accessible equivalent of a plot is a structured decision record, showing that this approach makes bioinformatics more inclusive, transparent, and auditable rather than simply accommodating accessibility as an afterthought.
AI.conclusion: Non-visual accessibility and computational reproducibility are closely aligned—both require transparent analyses that document why decisions were made. Treating accessibility as a requirement for decision documentation benefits all researchers by improving transparency and auditability while making the field more inclusive.

title: Extinction drives emergent metastability in complex ecosystems
summary: Extinction is inevitable; every species eventually dies out, impacting the ecosystem it is part of. Over the past few decades, extensive research stemming from the stability-diversity debate has addressed how species diversity contributes to the stability of large ecosystems. However, conventional stability criteria often rely on deterministic frameworks, overlooking the intrinsic population fluctuations that allow any species to go extinct by chance. In this paper, we incorporate demographic stochasticity into large complex ecosystems with a rule-based model. We demonstrate that such demographic fluctuations rapidly prune the low-abundance species from the ecological community, thereby securing higher systemic stability. By developing a bottom-up theory to characterise the statistics of extinction dynamics, we discover that the fraction of surviving species exhibits an anomalous heavy-tailed decay over time, revealing the emergence of remnant communities with robust metastability. Our results highlight that when demographic fluctuations are accounted for, ecosystems self-stabilise by reducing their diversity even when they are predicted to be chaotic in the deterministic limit.

AI.tldr: This paper incorporates demographic stochasticity into a rule-based model of large complex ecosystems, showing that demographic fluctuations rapidly prune low-abundance species, thereby securing higher systemic stability. The authors develop a bottom-up theory characterizing extinction statistics and discover that the fraction of surviving species exhibits anomalous heavy-tailed decay over time, revealing remnant communities with robust metastability. Their results show ecosystems self-stabilize by reducing diversity even when predicted to be chaotic in the deterministic limit.
AI.motivation: Conventional stability criteria in ecology rely on deterministic frameworks that overlook intrinsic population fluctuations allowing species to go extinct by chance. The authors aim to address this gap by incorporating demographic stochasticity into models of large complex ecosystems.
AI.method: The authors incorporate demographic stochasticity into a rule-based model of large complex ecosystems and develop a bottom-up theory to characterize the statistics of extinction dynamics.
AI.result: Demographic fluctuations rapidly prune low-abundance species, securing higher systemic stability. The fraction of surviving species exhibits anomalous heavy-tailed decay over time, revealing remnant communities with robust metastability. Ecosystems self-stabilize by reducing diversity even when predicted to be chaotic in the deterministic limit.
AI.conclusion: When demographic fluctuations are accounted for, ecosystems self-stabilise by reducing their diversity, which challenges the conventionally predicted chaotic behavior of such systems in deterministic frameworks.

title: BCIJelly: An integrated ecosystem for brain-computer interface research
comment: 67 pages, 6 figures, 7 extended data figures, 20 supplementary tables
summary: Brain-computer interface (BCI) research relies on multistage computational pipelines, yet progress remains constrained by fragmented data formats, heterogeneous decoder implementations and hardware-specific deployment toolchains, and researchers lack an integrated workflow. Here, we fill this gap with BCIJelly, a unified computational ecosystem that integrates 18 curated BCI datasets, 15 benchmark decoders and an algorithmic library of 80 reusable modules, an automated architecture search (AAS) procedure, and hardware-aware deployment through the toChip pipeline within a single Python framework. AAS constructs task-specific decoders without manual architecture design. It is further extended into a closed-loop mode guided by a large language model (LLM), which uses task specifications, module descriptions and search history to support multitask and cross-species decoding. The toChip pipeline compiles trained decoders for execution on neuromorphic chips, enabling energy-efficient deployment for BCI systems. An accompanying visualization software provides a graphical interface to the full workflow, making BCIJelly accessible without programming. We validate BCIJelly across five BCI paradigms (motor, visual, speech, emotion and auditory) with recordings from humans, macaques and mice, and single-task, multitask and cross-species decoding settings. BCIJelly establishes a unified and extensible infrastructure that bridges decoder development and hardware-aware deployment for BCI research.

AI.tldr: BCIJelly is a unified Python ecosystem for brain-computer interface (BCI) research that integrates 18 curated datasets, 15 benchmark decoders, 80 reusable modules, an automated architecture search (AAS) procedure with LLM-guided closed-loop extension, and a toChip pipeline for neuromorphic hardware deployment—validated across five BCI paradigms and multiple species.
AI.motivation: BCI research is hindered by fragmented data formats, heterogeneous decoder implementations, and hardware-specific deployment toolchains, with researchers lacking an integrated workflow that spans the entire pipeline.
AI.method: BCIJelly integrates curated datasets, benchmark decoders, and reusable algorithmic modules in a single Python framework. It employs automated architecture search (AAS) that can be extended into a closed-loop mode guided by a large language model (LLM) for multitask and cross-species decoding. The toChip pipeline compiles trained decoders for neuromorphic chip execution, and a visualization software provides a graphical interface to the full workflow.
AI.result: BCIJelly was validated across five BCI paradigms (motor, visual, speech, emotion, auditory) with recordings from humans, macaques, and mice, covering single-task, multitask, and cross-species decoding settings.
AI.conclusion: BCIJelly establishes a unified and extensible infrastructure that bridges decoder development and hardware-aware deployment for BCI research.

title: Classification of Intracellular Protein Patterns from Reactive Equilibria
comment: 22 pages main text, 17 pages Appendix, 13 figures
summary: Self-organized spatial patterns are central to nonequilibrium physics and cell biology, yet locating instabilities in multi-component, reaction-diffusion networks remains challenging because standard eigenvalue analyses scale with the number of biochemical states and rely on reaction kinetics often poorly constrained by experiments. Exploiting the common mass-conserving structure of protein reaction kinetics and the fact that nonlinear feedback is typically confined to membrane reactions while lateral membrane diffusion is negligible, we develop a geometric classification that predicts stationary, and approximately also oscillatory, pattern-forming instabilities from reactive equilibria. The developed criteria reduce the stability analysis from the full component space to the space of conserved species. On this reduced space, slope matrices---describing the change of equilibrium cytosolic densities with respect to total species densities---govern onset. Based on densities in chemical equilibrium, this approach eliminates the requirement of comprehensive kinetic knowledge frequently lacking in experimental systems. Thus, a broad range of instabilities can be understood as mass-redistribution instabilities---self-amplifying mass redistribution caused by shifting local equilibria. We apply these criteria to models for the Escherichia coli Min system and the Caenorhabditis elegans polarity system and show that the reduction extends to the mixed-dimensional dynamics in systems coupling bulk cytosolic dynamics with membrane dynamics on the boundary. Together, these results provide an interpretable, broadly applicable, and experimentally accessible framework for diagnosing and designing pattern formation in multicomponent nonequilibrium systems on the basis of conservation laws.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a geometric classification framework for predicting pattern-forming instabilities in multi-component reaction-diffusion systems by exploiting the common mass-conserving structure of protein reaction kinetics. The approach reduces stability analysis from the full component space to the space of conserved species, using slope matrices that describe how equilibrium cytosolic densities change with respect to total species densities. This eliminates the need for comprehensive kinetic knowledge and identifies instabilities as mass-redistribution instabilities. The framework is validated on E. coli Min system and C. elegans polarity models.
AI.motivation: Standard eigenvalue analyses for locating instabilities in multi-component reaction-diffusion networks scale poorly with the number of biochemical states and depend on reaction kinetics that are often poorly constrained by experiments. There is a need for an interpretable, broadly applicable, and experimentally accessible framework for diagnosing pattern formation in multicomponent nonequilibrium systems.
AI.method: The authors exploit: (1) the common mass-conserving structure of protein reaction kinetics, (2) the confinement of nonlinear feedback to membrane reactions, and (3) negligible lateral membrane diffusion. They develop geometric criteria that predict stationary and approximately oscillatory pattern-forming instabilities from reactive equilibria. The stability analysis is reduced from the full component space to the space of conserved species, where slope matrices describing changes in equilibrium cytosolic densities with respect to total species densities govern the onset of instabilities.
AI.result: The developed criteria successfully predict instabilities based on densities in chemical equilibrium, eliminating the need for comprehensive kinetic knowledge. Applications to the E. coli Min system and the C. elegans polarity system demonstrate that the reduction extends to mixed-dimensional dynamics coupling bulk cytosolic dynamics with membrane dynamics on the boundary.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an interpretable, broadly applicable, and experimentally accessible approach for diagnosing and designing pattern formation in multicomponent nonequilibrium systems, grounded in conservation laws rather than detailed reaction kinetics.

title: Spatial Message Passing in Language Space for Pathology Image Interpretation
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can generate pathological descriptions from histological images, but gigapixel Whole Slide Images (WSIs) exceed their visual context limits. The standard tiling workaround makes WSIs tractable yet severs the tissue neighborhoods that define tumor-stroma interfaces and morphology. We introduce Spatial Language Message Passing (SLMP), a framework that performs spatial reasoning entirely in language space, human-readable by construction. SLMP represents a WSI region as a spatial text graph: tiles are nodes initialized with MLLM descriptions, and edges encode spatial adjacency. For each tile, an LLM refines its description by integrating language messages from adjacent tiles under a shared aggregation policy that, on the tile grid, acts as an adaptive local kernel operating on text rather than learned embeddings. This policy is an inspectable prompt that can be refined from model-observed tissue phenotypes via textual gradients, enabling automatic semantic optimization from local cellular context to broader tissue morphology without fine-tuning MLLM weights. On representative HER2 and CAMELYON16 regions, SLMP improves tile-level tumor description accuracy in settings spanning general-purpose and pathology-specialized backbones, with gains of +3.3 to +19.6 percentage points. Random-neighbor ablations confirm that these gains stem from spatial context rather than additional text alone, and inspecting the optimized policies reveals interpretable, tissue-specific decision rules. Besides, without any weight updates or fine-tuning the backbone MLLM, SLMP substantially improves general-purpose MLLMs and narrows its gap to pathology-specialized counterparts, offering a transparent and flexible mechanism for incorporating spatial reasoning into MLLM-based pathology analysis.

AI.tldr: SLMP is a framework that enables spatial reasoning on gigapixel histopathology images entirely in language space, representing WSI regions as spatial text graphs where MLLM-generated tile descriptions are refined via LLM message passing under an interpretable aggregation policy, improving tumor description accuracy without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: WSIs exceed MLLM visual context limits, and the standard tiling approach severs tissue neighborhoods critical for defining tumor-stroma interfaces and morphology, leaving a gap in spatial reasoning for MLLM-based pathology analysis.
AI.method: SLMP represents a WSI region as a spatial text graph: tiles are nodes with MLLM descriptions, edges encode spatial adjacency. An LLM refines each tile's description by passing language messages from neighboring tiles under a shared aggregation policy that acts as an adaptive local kernel on text. The policy is an inspectable prompt refined via textual gradients from observed tissue phenotypes, requiring no weight updates.
AI.result: On HER2 and CAMELYON16 regions, SLMP improves tile-level tumor description accuracy by +3.3 to +19.6 percentage points across general-purpose and pathology-specialized backbones. Ablations confirm gains come from spatial context, and optimized policies reveal interpretable, tissue-specific rules. SLMP substantially narrows the gap between general-purpose and pathology-specialized MLLMs without fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Spatial reasoning over tissue neighborhoods can be performed transparently in language space, offering a flexible, human-inspectable mechanism to incorporate spatial context into MLLM-based pathology analysis without weight updates.

title: Absorbing phase transition in a queueing model of coupled adaptive agents
summary: What decides whether people do things together or separately? Many activities cannot be carried out alone, and an individual must rank them against the private tasks competing for the same time. We address this within the priority-queue description of human activity by letting each agent choose the priority of a shared task rather than drawing it from a fixed distribution: the value of the joint activity, discounted by the estimated risk that the partner will not take part. Participation becomes strategic, and the model acquires a phase transition. A coupled phase, in which joint activity is sustained, is separated from an absorbing solitary phase by a saddle-node bifurcation that we obtain in closed form. The transition is discontinuous and the solitary phase is absorbing, so collapse is irreversible unless an agent persists unilaterally for of order one memory time, a cost we also compute. The heavy-tailed interevent statistics that motivate queueing models of human dynamics survive only in a narrow window at the transition, and there the exponent is fixed by the fraction of time spent coupled rather than by queue length: the universality classes of the non-strategic model do not survive the introduction of choice. On a network, attention divides as $1/(k+a)$ and fixes a critical degree beyond which no coupled state exists, so the solitary phase percolates according to the Molloy--Reed criterion with the second moment truncated at that degree --- formally an attack on hubs, with no attacker. For group activities the critical degree falls as the $(m-1)$th root, implying a maximum group size. The transition organises two quantities already measured in communication records: a finite capacity for keeping ties active, and the decay of ties whose rhythm is interrupted.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a strategic model of joint vs. solitary activity by extending the priority-queue framework of human dynamics. Individuals decide whether to participate in shared tasks by weighing the value of joint activity against the estimated probability that their partner will also participate. This introduces a phase transition between a coupled (joint activity) phase and an absorbing solitary phase, separated by a saddle-node bifurcation obtained in closed form. The transition is discontinuous and irreversible without prolonged unilateral persistence. Heavy-tailed interevent statistics survive only in a narrow window at the transition with universality classes changed. On networks, attention divides as 1/(k+a), yielding a critical degree; while for group activities a maximum group size emerges.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks to understand the fundamental question of what determines whether individuals engage in activities together or separately, particularly when shared tasks compete with private tasks for limited time. It extends the standard priority-queue model of human dynamics where task priorities are drawn from fixed distributions, to a strategic setting where participation is a choice, in order to explain empirically observed phenomena like finite capacity for maintaining active ties and the decay of interrupted ties.
AI.method: The authors generalize the priority-queue model of human activity by letting each agent choose the priority assigned to a shared task rather than drawing it from a fixed distribution. The chosen priority reflects the value of joint activity discounted by the estimated risk that the partner will not participate. Strategic choice creates a feedback loop that produces a phase transition. The saddle-node bifurcation separating the coupled and solitary phases is derived in closed form, and the analysis extends to networks and group activities.
AI.result: The model exhibits a discontinuous phase transition between a coupled phase and an absorbing solitary phase via a saddle-node bifurcation. The transition is irreversible without persistent unilateral action lasting on the order of one memory time, with the associated cost computed. Heavy-tailed interevent statistics persist only in a narrow window at the transition, with the exponent fixed by the coupling fraction rather than queue length, breaking the universality classes of the non-strategic model. On networks, attention scales as 1/(k+a), giving a critical degree, and the solitary phase percolates per the Molloy-Reed criterion with truncated second moment. Group activities yield a maximum group size where the critical degree falls as the (m-1)th root.
AI.conclusion: The introduction of strategic choice fundamentally alters the priority-queue description of human activity, producing an irreversible absorbing-state transition. The model unifies two empirically observed quantities in communication records: the finite capacity for maintaining active ties and the decay of ties whose rhythm is interrupted. The results also imply that the universality classes of the non-strategic model do not survive strategic decision-making.

title: Length scale of cellular activity determines signatures of epithelial remodeling
summary: Cellular activity drives epithelial fluidization --- a widespread phenomenon observed during tissue development, remodeling, and repair both in vivo and in vitro. Yet the physical origins and spatial organization of active forces vary widely across biological systems and are often represented by a single generic mechanism in theoretical models. Here, using an active vertex model, we systematically compare four modes of epithelial activity spanning subcellular to tissue scales: apolar motility, polar motility, fluctuating contractility, and mechanochemical regulation. Although all four mechanisms drive the same global transition from a solid-like rectangular tissue to a fluid-like circular morphology, they reach this state through distinct pathways --- differing in the rates and topology of junctional rearrangements, cell elimination, and collective motion and leave distinguishable signatures in tissue architecture, cell dynamics, and mechanical relaxation. Among these observables, spatial velocity correlations directly capture the spatial organization of activity: their correlation length and functional form together resolve all four mechanisms. The robustness of these signatures across activity strengths suggests that spatial velocity correlations offer an experimentally accessible means of identifying the physical origin of epithelial activity from live-cell imaging alone.

AI.tldr: Using an active vertex model, the paper systematically compares four modes of epithelial activity (apolar motility, polar motility, fluctuating contractility, and mechanochemical regulation). Although all four drive the same solid-to-fluid transition, they produce distinct signatures in junctional rearrangements, cell elimination, collective motion, and mechanical relaxation. Spatial velocity correlations uniquely resolve all four mechanisms, offering an experimentally accessible way to identify active force origins from live-cell imaging.
AI.motivation: Epithelial fluidization is widespread in development and repair, but the physical origins and spatial organization of active forces vary widely across systems and are often oversimplified as a single generic mechanism in theoretical models. A systematic comparison is needed to distinguish how different activity modes drive the same macroscopic transition.
AI.method: The authors employ an active vertex model to systematically compare four modes of epithelial activity: apolar motility, polar motility, fluctuating contractility, and mechanochemical regulation. They analyze the resulting tissue architecture, cell dynamics, mechanical relaxation, and spatial velocity correlations.
AI.result: All four activity mechanisms drive the same global solid-to-fluid transition (rectangular to circular morphology), but via distinct pathways that differ in the rates and topology of junctional rearrangements, cell elimination, and collective motion. Each leaves distinguishable signatures in tissue architecture, cell dynamics, and mechanical relaxation. Spatial velocity correlations, through their correlation length and functional form, uniquely resolve all four mechanisms, and these signatures are robust across activity strengths.
AI.conclusion: Spatial velocity correlations provide an experimentally accessible means to identify the physical origin of epithelial activity from live-cell imaging alone, enabling mechanistic discrimination among different active force generation modes.
